summary.text: An exhaustive check for \(1\le d\le2025\) shows that one of \((11,13),(7,19),(5,29),(7,13),(7,11),(3,47),(2,73)\) consists of two primes neither dividing \(d\); in every pair the primes have different final digits and product at most \(150\). Thus \(d\) is invertible modulo their product \(pq\), so some \(0\le i<pq\le150\) satisfies \(pq\mid a+id\), forcing one of the first 150 terms to have prime divisors with different final digits.

full_proof.text:
Call an integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same residue modulo \(10\). We prove that there cannot be an increasing arithmetic progression
\[
 a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
with \(a\ge 2\), \(1\le d\le 2025\), and all 150 terms lopsided.

We first record the mechanism that will produce a non-lopsided term.

**Modular lemma.** Let \(p\) and \(q\) be distinct primes such that
\[
pq\le 150,
\]
and suppose neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\). Then, for every integer \(a\), one of the 150 terms \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), is divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\).

Indeed, since \(p\nmid d\) and \(q\nmid d\), and \(p,q\) are distinct primes, we have
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Thus multiplication by \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\). If \(d^{-1}\) denotes an inverse of \(d\) modulo \(pq\), choose \(i\) to be the least nonnegative residue of
\[
-a d^{-1}\pmod{pq}.
\]
Then
\[
0\le i<pq\le 150
\]
and
\[
a+id\equiv a-a d^{-1}d\equiv 0\pmod{pq}.
\]
Therefore \(pq\mid a+id\), so both \(p\) and \(q\) divide that term. Since \(i<pq\le150\), this is one of the indices \(0,1,\ldots,149\), as required.

If, in addition, \(p\) and \(q\) have different final decimal digits, the term furnished by the modular lemma cannot be lopsided: it has the two prime divisors \(p\) and \(q\), while
\[
p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}.
\]
The condition \(a\ge2\) ensures that every term \(a+id\) is positive, so there is no exceptional zero term to consider.

We now show that every possible common difference \(d\) in the prescribed range admits a prime pair to which this lemma applies. Consider the following pairs:
\[
(11,13),\quad (7,19),\quad (5,29),\quad (7,13),\quad
(7,11),\quad (3,47),\quad (2,73).
\]
Every entry is prime. The products and final decimal digits are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
(p,q)&pq&(p\bmod 10,q\bmod 10)\\ \hline
(11,13)&143&(1,3)\\
(7,19)&133&(7,9)\\
(5,29)&145&(5,9)\\
(7,13)&91&(7,3)\\
(7,11)&77&(7,1)\\
(3,47)&141&(3,7)\\
(2,73)&146&(2,3).
\end{array}
\]
Thus every product is at most \(150\), and the two primes in each pair have different final digits.

We claim that if \(1\le d\le2025\), then at least one of these pairs \((p,q)\) has the property that neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\). Suppose, for a contradiction, that there were no such pair. Negating “neither prime divides \(d\)” for each pair says that at least one member of every pair must divide \(d\). In particular, using six of the seven pairs above, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
&11\mid d\quad\hbox{or}\quad 13\mid d,\\
&5\mid d\quad\hbox{or}\quad 29\mid d,\\
&7\mid d\quad\hbox{or}\quad 13\mid d,\\
&7\mid d\quad\hbox{or}\quad 11\mid d,\\
&3\mid d\quad\hbox{or}\quad 47\mid d,\\
&2\mid d\quad\hbox{or}\quad 73\mid d.
\end{aligned}
\]
(The unused clause \(7\mid d\) or \(19\mid d\), coming from the pair \((7,19)\), is not even needed for the bound.)

The three clauses involving \(7,11,13\), namely
\[
11\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d,\qquad
7\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d,\qquad
7\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d,
\]
force at least two of the three primes \(7,11,13\) to divide \(d\). To see this explicitly, there are two cases.

* If \(7\nmid d\), then the second and third clauses force both \(13\mid d\) and \(11\mid d\).
* If \(7\mid d\), then the first clause forces at least one of \(11\) and \(13\) to divide \(d\), in addition to \(7\).

Consequently, \(d\) is divisible by the product of two distinct members of \(\{7,11,13\}\). The smallest possible such product is
\[
7\cdot11=77;
\]
the other possibilities are \(7\cdot13=91\) and \(11\cdot13=143\).

The remaining three clauses allow us to select primes
\[
r\in\{2,73\},\qquad s\in\{3,47\},\qquad t\in\{5,29\}
\]
such that each of \(r,s,t\) divides \(d\). They satisfy
\[
r\ge2,\qquad s\ge3,\qquad t\ge5.
\]
These three primes are distinct from one another and from \(7,11,13\). Therefore the five selected, pairwise distinct primes all divide \(d\). Since distinct primes are pairwise coprime, their product divides \(d\). As \(d>0\), this gives
\[
d\ge r s t\cdot(\text{the selected product of two primes from }\{7,11,13\}).
\]
Using the lower bounds just obtained,
\[
d\ge 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot77=2310.
\]
This contradicts \(d\le2025\). Hence the claim is proved: for every \(1\le d\le2025\), at least one pair in the displayed list consists of two primes that both fail to divide \(d\).

Now suppose that the conjectured progression existed. Apply the claim to its common difference \(d\), and choose an available pair \((p,q)\). There are seven possible cases, corresponding to the seven listed pairs. In each case:

1. \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct primes;
2. neither divides \(d\);
3. \(pq\le150\); and
4. \(p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}\).

By the modular lemma, there is an index \(i\) with \(0\le i<150\) such that
\[
pq\mid a+id.
\]
Thus both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime divisors of \(a+id\). The table shows in each of the seven cases that these two prime divisors have different final decimal digits. Hence \(a+id\) is not lopsided. This contradicts the assumption that every one of the 150 terms is a number whose prime divisors all share the same final decimal digit.

Therefore no integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) can have all of
\[
a+id\qquad(0\le i<150)
\]
in A381159. The proposed existence assertion is false.
